node.label: Frederick Jackson Turner
node.date_label: “The Significance of the Frontier in American History” (1893) · Rise of the New West (1906) · The Frontier in American History (1920)
node.description: A historian whose frontier interpretation linked western settlement to American institutions and democracy. His presidential address also called for historians to combine economic, political, geographical and social inquiries. The settler-centred language of available land is his historical premise, with Indigenous dispossession obscured by that formulation.

proposed_edges.relationship: Explains American political development through western settlement and changing social forces.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary frontier opening and 1910 address ground the interpretation; “free land” is a settler premise that obscures Indigenous sovereignty.

proposed_edges.relationship: Calls for combined economic, political, geographic and social inquiry rather than isolated specialist explanations.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read 1910 address explicitly argues that human social factors are varied and complex; no claim Turner founded later comparative historical sociology.
